findings.paper_title: Item 16 - Contract and Financial Procedure Matters
findings.headline: Infinity Park Enterprise Zone business rates (£0.646m in 2026/27, forecast £0.777m in 2027/28) retained by Derby through 31 March 2041, moving from EMCCA passporting to direct council management.
findings.detail: Derby is taking direct ownership of business rates generated within the Infinity Park Enterprise Zone, with forecasts of £0.646m in 2026/27 and £0.777m in 2027/28, continuing through March 2041. A new reserve 'IPD Retained Business Rates' will manage these funds; 2026/27 expenditure is planned at £0.372m for existing commitments and £0.274m for feasibility works on pipeline projects (Infinity HQ, Technology Hub, power infrastructure), with any surplus retained in reserve.
findings.matters: Councils securing long-term ring-fenced revenue streams from strategic regeneration sites demonstrate how they fund capital infrastructure investment. For lenders, this shows tangible revenue sources supporting capital commitments. For peer councils, this illustrates governance structures for managing designated zone revenues.
findings.figures: Business rates income £0.646m in 2026/27, forecast £0.777m in 2027/28, policy active until 31 March 2041, feasibility work allocation up to £0.500m
findings.quote: Participation in the EZ and designation of a BRR site provides the opportunity for the Council to secure and re-invest 100% of IPD business rates generated until March 2041.

findings.paper_title: Item 16 - Contract and Financial Procedure Matters
findings.headline: Morleston Short Break Centre capital scheme increases from £2.638m to £3.322m with project redirected from refurbishment to demolition and new build.
findings.detail: The scheme for relocating the Bonsall View short breaks service (approved January 2026) has been fundamentally redirected. The original budget of £2.638m for refurbishment has become £3.322m for demolition and new build, an increase of £0.684m (26%). The change follows assessment that the existing building is unsuitable for long-term service delivery due to condition, layout and structural limitations. Capital costs of £0.085m incurred on the original refurbishment proposal have been written off as abortive. The revised budget is profiled £0.671m in 2026/27 and £2.651m in 2027/28, to be funded from existing property budgets.
findings.matters: Councils and lenders track capital project escalations and mid-project redirects as indicators of execution risk. A scheme approved less than a year ago now requires a 26% budget increase and fundamental change of approach, signalling either inadequate initial assessment or unforeseen conditions that other councils managing similar projects will want to monitor.
findings.figures: Original budget £2.638m, revised budget £3.322m, increase £0.684m (26%), abortive costs £0.085m
findings.quote: Capital costs of £0.085m incurred in relation to the original refurbishment proposal have been identified as abortive following the decision (if approved) to proceed with the alternative scheme (demolition and new build).

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: Council tax increase 4.99% to £1,898.99 Band D, at maximum allowable rate
findings.detail: Derby is applying a 4.99% council tax increase for 2026/27, raising Band D to £1,898.99. This is at the maximum permitted level and matches Leicester. Nottingham is increasing at 3.5% and Coventry at 3.9%. The council notes that government core spending calculations assume councils maximise tax levies, so accepting less than 4.99% would reduce spending power further.
findings.matters: A council at maximum tax increases signals constraint by legislation rather than restraint. This typically precedes requests to government for additional flexibility or funding and indicates limited scope to raise revenue locally.
findings.figures: Council tax increase 4.99%, Band D £1,898.99; Leicester 4.99%; Nottingham 3.5%; Coventry 3.9%
findings.quote: Government core spending calculations are based on council's maximising their council tax levies so by not applying the maximum council tax increase allowable it will not see the maximum real terms increase in spending power, this will limit its ability to fund essential services

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: £7.105m permanent budget savings required in 2026/27 with delivery risk flagged
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget requires delivery of £7.105m permanent savings to achieve balance. The council flags this as a material risk: 'The risk of not delivering these savings is being monitored and reported to Cabinet. Risk within these plans must be mitigated by directors owning and delivering their savings commitments or identifying alternative delivery savings.' This continues a pattern of large annual savings dependency; since 2010/11 the council has delivered £261m cumulative savings.
findings.matters: Councils dependent on ongoing large savings delivery face execution risk; failure to deliver can quickly create deficits. The fact that such savings are flagged as a material risk suggests confidence in full delivery is not complete.
findings.figures: Required permanent savings 2026/27 £7.105m; cumulative savings since 2010/11 £261m
findings.quote: the budget for 2026/27 required permanent budget savings of £7.105m to be delivered to bring the budget into balance. The risk of not delivering these savings is being monitored and reported to Cabinet

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: Capital programme increased to £227.272m with 29% (c.£66m) funded by unsupported borrowing
findings.detail: The capital programme forecast has increased from £220.538m approved to £227.272m at Q1 2026/27. Funding sources: 53% Government Grants (c.£120m), 29% Unsupported Borrowing (c.£66m), 6% Capital Receipts, 7% Major Repairs Allowance, with minor contributions from reserves, direct revenue, Section 106 and external contributions. The council notes that 'the future capital programme will continue to be reviewed to reduce the forecast level of borrowing', indicating concern at current unsupported borrowing levels and their revenue impact.
findings.matters: Capital programme growth funded by increased borrowing shifts risk onto the revenue budget through debt servicing. A council signalling intent to reduce borrowing is making an explicit tradeoff between capital ambitions and revenue sustainability.
findings.figures: Capital programme Q1 2026/27 forecast £227.272m; Unsupported Borrowing 29% (c.£66m); Government Grants 53% (c.£120m)
findings.quote: The capital expenditure forecast as at Qtr. 1 is £227.272m...The future capital programme will continue to be reviewed to reduce the forecast level of borrowing and maintain an affordable and sustainable capital programme

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: Q1 2026/27 revenue forecast minimal overspend but masks £3.228m emerging pressure in People Services
findings.detail: While the council achieved a Q1 2026/27 overall revenue position of £0.234m overspend (minimal and manageable), this masks emerging pressures of £3.228m within People Services. This reflects ongoing demand-led pressures in adult social care, children's services, and homelessness support. The council has invested £25.445m in Adult Social Care over three years to address rising demand and cost pressures, but demand continues to grow at pace driven by demographic change and increasing complexity of need.
findings.matters: People Services are typically a council's largest and most volatile cost area. Q1 emerging pressures are a leading indicator for full-year position and medium-term trajectory. Demand-led pressures that persist despite significant investment suggest underlying mismatch between resources and need.
findings.figures: Q1 2026/27 emerging pressures in Peoples Directorate £3.228m; investment in Adult Social Care over 3 years £25.445m
findings.quote: the forecast revenue position for Derby is a £0.234m overspend which is minimal and can be managed within existing resources. However within this figure there are still emerging pressures in the Peoples Directorate of £3.228m...demand for services continues to grow at pace

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: General Fund reserves recovered by £4.066m from 2025/26 underspend, first underspend in several years
findings.detail: Derby delivered a £4.066m General Fund underspend in 2025/26, transferred to reserves. This is the first underspend in several years, representing a turning point in financial resilience after a long period of depletion. The council targets reserves at 3–5% of net budget expenditure. Historically depleted reserves have constrained capacity to absorb demand volatility and unexpected costs.
findings.matters: A council moving from consistent deficits to underspends signals improved financial discipline and provides building blocks for resilience. This improves capacity to manage service volatility and unexpected costs.
findings.figures: 2025/26 General Fund underspend £4.066m transferred to reserves; first underspend in several years
findings.quote: The Council is on a journey to rebuild its financial resilience and has made some really good progress strengthening its General Fund reserves and managing its spending throughout the year, which created an underspend in 2025/26 for the first time in a number of years

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: Waste Treatment Centre impairment of £51.407m requires government Capitalisation Directive
findings.detail: The decision not to proceed with operation of the Derby and Derbyshire Waste Treatment Centre triggers an impairment and write-back of approximately £51.407m. This is not new cash cost but an accounting consequence of the facility no longer generating expected future economic benefits. The scale requires the Director of Finance to seek a Capitalisation Directive from government to manage the revenue implications.
findings.matters: A £51m impairment is material and unusual; a Capitalisation Directive is a rare government intervention signalling severe accounting pressures. The event indicates a major capital investment outcome fundamentally not materialising as planned.
findings.figures: Impairment and write-back impact c.£51.407m
findings.quote: requires current estimates indicating an impairment and write-back impact for the City Council of approximately £51.407m...The Director of Finance and Section 151 Officer is required to seek a Capitalisation Directive

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit £33.247m; government grant of c.£21m leaves c.£12.2m funding gap
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit stands at £33.247m, with in-year deficit forecast at £9.973m for 2026/27. Government is providing a High Needs Stability Grant to cover approximately 90% of historic SEND deficits accrued to 31 March 2026, representing c.£21m cash for Derby. However, a forecast gap of c.£12.2m remains and must be incorporated into the financial plan. The DSG statutory override has been extended to April 2028, allowing the deficit to be excluded from usable reserves for statutory accounting purposes.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are a chronic issue across English local government. Movement in this position and level of government support directly affects reserve sustainability and the long-term service delivery model for special needs.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £33.247m; government grant c.£21m; outstanding gap c.£12.2m; in-year forecast deficit 2026/27 £9.973m
findings.quote: In February 2026, the government pledged £5 billion to cover up to 90% of the historic SEND deficits accrued by Councils to the end of 2025/26. This represents a circa £21m replenishment of cash flow for the city...However there is still a forecast gap of circa £12.2m

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: Fair Funding Settlement enables first balanced three-year budget in several years
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Reforms 2026 reset core government funding allocation, replacing historic patterns with need-based distribution. Derby benefited significantly, moving to structural balance over the medium term after years of cumulative deficits. The settlement allocates higher resources to authorities with greater social care demand, deprivation and lower local revenue bases. The council describes the outcome as allowing it to invest significantly into services for the first time in a long period.
findings.matters: A council achieving structural balance for the first time in years has moved from cumulative deficit management to financial sustainability. This fundamentally changes its fiscal flexibility and resilience, and signals whether funding reforms are delivering their intended effect.
findings.figures: Budget gap progression: 2027/28 £1.826m, 2028/29 £1.690m, 2029/30 (£0.057m) surplus
findings.quote: Derby faired very well from those reforms allowing the Council to set a balanced budget over the medium term, for the first time in several years

findings.paper_title: Item 15 - Council Tax Long-Term Empty Homes and Second Homes Premiums
findings.headline: Full Council must decide by 31 March 2027 to implement long-term empty homes premium from April 2027; second homes decision required by 1 April 2028.
findings.detail: Statutory requirements impose specific deadlines for the council's decision-making. For long-term empty homes, the premium must be determined before the start of the financial year in which it applies, requiring a Full Council decision by 31 March 2027 to enable April 2027 implementation. For second homes, as a first determination, the decision must be made at least one year before implementation, requiring decision by 1 April 2028 to enable April 2028 implementation.
findings.matters: Implementation deadlines are statutory requirements; missing them delays income realisation and requires restarting the governance process, affecting budget planning and revenue forecasting.
findings.figures: Decision deadline for long-term empty homes: 31 March 2027; Decision deadline for second homes: 1 April 2028; Consultation period: 9 October 2026 to 31 December 2026
findings.quote: A Full Council decision by 31 March 2027 would therefore enable the proposed commencement dates of 1 April 2027 and 1 April 2028 respectively

findings.paper_title: Item 15 - Council Tax Long-Term Empty Homes and Second Homes Premiums
findings.headline: Council proposes Council Tax premiums on empty homes and second homes expected to yield approximately £950k annually (illustrative 2024 figure, to be refreshed).
findings.detail: The council proposes a 100% Council Tax premium on long-term empty homes (after one year of continuous vacancy, from April 2027) and a 100% premium on second homes (from April 2028). Illustrative modelling based on a February 2024 property snapshot projected combined gross additional Council Tax revenue of £975,204.72 with ultimate collection of £949,849.40 at 97.4% collection rate, though these figures are not current forecasts and will be refreshed following consultation. Council Tax income is shared between the council and its major preceptors through the Collection Fund, so the full amount does not accrue solely to Derby.
findings.matters: Under budget pressures, councils seek new revenue sources; this proposal targets a material potential income stream from underutilised housing, though actual yield depends on consultation findings, final property counts, and statutory exemptions.
findings.figures: Gross additional Council Tax revenue (illustrative, February 2024): £975,204.72; Ultimate collection at 97.4%: £949,849.40. Long-term empty homes: £705,847.81 gross (£687,495.77 ultimate). Second homes: £269,356.91 gross (£262,353.63 ultimate)
findings.quote: combined gross additional Council Tax of £975,204.72 before statutory exceptions and non-collection, with illustrative ultimate collection of £949,849.40. These figures are not a current forecast for 2027/28 or 2028/29

findings.paper_title: Item 15 - Council Tax Long-Term Empty Homes and Second Homes Premiums
findings.headline: Governance error in 2024 approval process corrected, with approximately £459k in refunds to be issued to affected taxpayers.
findings.detail: An earlier 2024 process contained an administrative error resulting in Council Tax premiums being charged without a valid Full Council determination, though the council is now correcting this through refunds. Long-term empty homes premiums totalling £1.2m were charged, of which £315k has been collected and will be refunded; second homes premiums totalling £553k were charged, of which £144k will be refunded, totalling approximately £459k in estimated cash refunds. Funding has been ringfenced to meet these costs.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer councils monitor governance and internal control effectiveness; this error represents a control weakness but the corrective action demonstrates the council's ability to identify and remediate audit-type issues, though at material cost.
findings.figures: Long-term empty homes: £1.2m charged, £315k collected (refund liability); Second homes: £553k charged, £144k collected (refund liability); Total estimated cash refund liability: approximately £459k
findings.quote: owing to an administrative error, the subsequent report did not complete the required approval route, and no valid Full Council determination was made

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Procurement of the Framework Agreement for Adult Care Home Provisions
findings.headline: Council absorbing new framework transition and dementia cost premiums within existing Adult Social Care budget without additional funding
findings.detail: The council states transition to the new framework will operate within existing Adult Social Care budgets with no additional funding sought. Standard residential and nursing fees will mirror current rates for existing placements. Dementia cost premiums apply to new placements only, with overall financial impact managed through future budget monitoring and volume forecasting.
findings.matters: Budget absorptability and cost management approaches indicate financial health and sustainability. This shows the council managing emerging cost pressures through targeted design rather than blanket funding increases, with forward risk management through volume forecasting.
findings.figures: No additional funding sought; standard residential and standard nursing fees maintained at current rates
findings.quote: The proposed framework will operate within the Council's existing Adult Social Care residential and nursing care budget. Standard residential and standard nursing fees will mirror the current rates for existing placements, and no additional funding is sought to transition existing placements to the new contractual arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Procurement of the Framework Agreement for Adult Care Home Provisions
findings.headline: Council establishing 10-year framework valued at £447.2m for independent adult care home placements supporting 1,287 people
findings.detail: The new procurement establishes a 10-year Framework Agreement with combined value of £447.2m reflecting total expenditure on placements over the term. Current position (2025/26): £44.7m annual spend, 1,287 people across 221 settings, approximately 900 long-term placements funded at any point. The framework replaces long-outdated contractual arrangements across this material budget area.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of major multi-year budget commitments. The scale and duration of this care home framework makes it material to financial planning. Council care home spending is a substantial, ongoing commitment that directly affects medium-term budget capacity.
findings.figures: £447,222,030.40 total framework value; £44,722,203.04 annual spend (2025/26); 1,287 people in 221 care home settings; approximately 900 long-term placements
findings.quote: For information, during the financial year 2025/26 the Council supported 1,287 people in 221 care home settings to the value of £44,722,203.04 net cost per annum. There are on average 900 long-term care home placements being funded at any point in time by the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Procurement of the Framework Agreement for Adult Care Home Provisions
findings.headline: Council introducing 8.7% and 9.5% cost premiums for dementia care placements citing placement securing difficulties
findings.detail: The new 10-year framework introduces higher fees for dementia-specific care due to supply constraints and elevated costs. Residential Dementia placements will cost 8.7% more than standard residential, Nursing Dementia 9.5% more than standard nursing—amounting to approximately £62.52 and £70.10 additional cost per week respectively. The council explicitly cites current difficulties securing suitable placements as justification.
findings.matters: Councils facing similar care home capacity constraints need to understand how peers manage cost pressures through pricing. Dementia care cost inflation is a significant trend in social care markets, and this shows a material cost driver in a £44.7m annual budget.
findings.figures: 8.7% for Residential Dementia and 9.5% for Nursing Dementia; approximately £62.52 per week for Residential Dementia and £70.10 per week for Nursing Dementia
findings.quote: The model introduces new premiums of 8.7% for Residential Dementia and 9.5% for Nursing Dementia, reflecting the additional costs of Dementia care and current difficulties the Council experiences securing suitable placements.

findings.headline: Strong visitor footfall (16,000 weekly, 51,000 Christmas period) not converting to forecast income levels
findings.detail: The venue is attracting significant visitor numbers: averaging 16,000 per week in November 2025 and 51,000 over Christmas 2025. This demonstrates the venue functions as a destination and validates the capital investment. However, strong footfall has not translated into the rental income and trader turnover assumed in the business case, indicating either pricing issues, occupancy constraints limiting conversion, or trader operational difficulties affecting sales and rent payments.
findings.matters: Footfall is a leading indicator of venue success and potential, but revenue conversion (footfall to income) is what matters financially; strong demand that doesn't convert to revenue suggests business model, pricing, or offer issues that require operational correction
findings.figures: 16,000 average weekly visitors (November 2025); 51,000 visitors over Christmas 2025 period
findings.quote: Figures from November 2025 indicated that an average of 16,000 people a week are visiting the Market Hall, and 51,000 people visited over the Christmas 2025 period

findings.headline: Council to undertake structured options appraisal of market hall operating models including outsourcing
findings.detail: The commercial review recommends that council undertake soft market testing and a structured options appraisal of operating models including in-house (current model), hybrid arrangements, and outsourced models; alongside a time-limited 'prove and review' period for an improved in-house model. This reflects underlying concerns about whether the current in-house model has sufficient commercial capability, financial discipline, and operating focus. The recommendation signals that the operating model is not viewed as settled or optimal.
findings.matters: Operating model choice affects financial risk allocation, subsidy requirement, and governance; the fact that alternatives are being formally appraised suggests material questions about the current approach's viability and risk profile
findings.figures: No financial figures provided; this is a forward-looking recommendation
findings.quote: The review also recommends that the Council undertakes soft market testing and a structured options appraisal of operating models (including in-house, hybrid and outsourced approaches), alongside a time-limited 'prove and review' period for an improved in-house model

findings.headline: Bad debt provisions in original model set at relatively low level for early years
findings.detail: The business case included bad debt assumptions that the reviewer assesses as too low for a new, high-churn market operation. Bad debt typically starts high as new traders establish themselves and stabilize over time. The under-provisioning means actual write-offs are likely to exceed budgeted allowances, further eroding income performance and creating unbudgeted cost.
findings.matters: Bad debt is a material risk to revenue projections in new or high-turnover operations; under-provisioning masks true financial position and affects subsidy forecasts
findings.figures: No specific provision amounts provided in the paper
findings.quote: Bad debt provisions in the original model appear to have been set at a relatively low level for the early years, and would typically be expected to be higher at the outset and reduce over time as the operation stabilises

findings.headline: Invoice and rent collection processes not operational at opening; increases bad debt risk
findings.detail: Systems for regular invoicing, utilities billing, and service charge collection were not in place when the venue opened. This led to delayed invoices, backdated billing to traders, confusion and relationship damage, and increased bad debt risk. The council has since implemented monthly billing and regular finance meetings, but this represents a significant governance gap: a commercial operation should not open without complete financial transaction systems. The delay in implementing controls contributed to both financial loss and operational friction.
findings.matters: Financial control and timely cash collection are fundamental to council revenue management; opening a commercial operation without these systems represents elevated risk of receivables loss and reputational damage with tenants
findings.figures: No quantified impact provided; timing of improvements not specified
findings.quote: At the outset, processes and systems for regular billing of rent, utilities and storage charges were not fully in place. These issues have since been addressed, with: Monthly billing now in place. A regular finance meeting involving the Market Hall team, estates, finance and debt recovery

findings.headline: Occupancy and trader churn lower than forecast; venue now more subsidy-dependent than planned
findings.detail: While opening-day occupancy targets were achieved (50% non-food, 100% food stalls), early trading has produced higher trader churn than anticipated and under-occupancy in some areas. The paper notes this is a normal feature of market operations but the extent has contributed to financial underperformance. As a result, 'the operation is currently more reliant on subsidy than originally envisaged', indicating the business case assumption of self-sustaining operation within forecast timescale is not materializing.
findings.matters: Occupancy and tenant stability are leading indicators of venue viability, directly affect income, and determine subsidy duration and level; early churn suggests either pricing issues, operational problems, or market positioning challenges that affect sustainability
findings.figures: Business case: 50% non-food, 100% food occupancy assumed at opening; achieved on opening day; subsequently declined
findings.quote: This has been compounded by under-occupancy in some areas, an imbalanced trader mix, and weaknesses in invoicing, income management and lease processes. As a result, the operation is currently more reliant on subsidy than originally envisaged

findings.headline: First-year operating deficit exceeded £523,000 business case forecast
findings.detail: The business case forecast a deficit of £523k reducing to £107k in year 3. First-year actual operating costs were materially higher than budgeted. The paper does not quantify the actual year 1 deficit but attributes the overrun to three causes: lower-than-expected rental income (driven by occupancy shortfalls and trader churn), rent incentives offered to attract tenants, and higher event spending. This suggests the recovery trajectory assumed in the business case is not being met.
findings.matters: Revenue forecast accuracy is critical to council subsidy planning and financial management; material misses against forecast in year 1 of a new operation raise questions about the quality of underlying assumptions and the sustainability trajectory
findings.figures: Forecast deficit £523k year 1, £107k year 3; actual year 1 deficit not specified but stated as 'higher than budgeted'
findings.quote: In the first year of trading, the Market Hall's net cost was higher than budgeted, driven largely by lower than expected rental and commercial income and higher event spend

findings.headline: Market hall capital project delivered within £35m approved budget
findings.detail: The £35m refurbishment of Derby Market Hall's Grade II* listed building was completed within the approved budget and opened in May 2025. The project successfully delivered its capital objectives: creating a new visitor destination, securing the historic building's future, providing flexible event and market space, and improving city centre connectivity. This represents successful project delivery and completion of a major capital asset.
findings.matters: Delivery of major capital schemes on budget is a key measure of council project management and governance; equally, outcomes of that investment directly affect subsequent revenue sustainability
findings.figures: £35 million approved budget; final budget change February 2022; opened May 2025
findings.quote: With a capital budget of £35 million, and following the final budget change in February 2022, the project has been delivered within its approved budget, with the venue opening in May 2025

findings.headline: Net borrowing position fell by £20.629m in Q1 to £451.247m as investment balances grew
findings.detail: The Council's net borrowing position (total borrowing less investments and cash) decreased from £471.876m at 31 March 2026 to £451.247m at 30 June 2026. While total borrowing declined only slightly by £6.421m (with reclassification of maturing loans from long-term to short-term), this was more than offset by a £14.208m increase in investment balances. The investment growth primarily reflects the timing of grant receipts and council tax and business rates collection concentrated in early quarters, rather than debt reduction.
findings.matters: Quarterly swings in net borrowing position reflect cash management and timing of income; distinguishing between genuine debt reduction and cash balancing is important for assessing underlying debt trends and sustainability.
findings.figures: Net borrowing: £471.876m (31/03/2026) to £451.247m (30/06/2026), reduction of £20.629m. Gross borrowing decreased £6.421m; investments increased £14.208m from £109.682m to £123.890m
findings.quote: Net Borrowing Position 471.876 (20.629) 451.247

findings.headline: Bank of England held Bank Rate steady at 3.75% with expectation to remain at current elevated level
findings.detail: During Q1, the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee held Bank Rate steady at 3.75% throughout the quarter. The voting split shifted from 9-0 to hold in March to 7-2 by June, indicating some debate, but the Committee believes spare capacity in the economy can absorb price pressures without persistent inflation. The Council's treasury advisors (Arlingclose) maintain their central view that Bank Rate will remain at 3.75% despite expectations that inflation may rise to 3.5-4.0% from July.
findings.matters: Stable but elevated interest rates affect the cost of new borrowing and reinvestment returns on treasury investments; expected sustained high rates influence treasury strategy and borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: Bank Rate held at 3.75%. PWLB rates during Q1: 5-year maturity 5.04%-5.49%; 20-year maturity 6.02%-6.50%; 50-year maturity 5.89%-6.35%
findings.quote: the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) instead held Bank Rate steady throughout the quarter

findings.headline: Capital programme of £226.272m for 2026/27 led by Our City Our River (£78.383m) and schools investments (£73.001m)
findings.detail: The Council has a substantial capital programme with £226.272m planned spending in 2026/27 (General Fund £177.419m, HRA £48.853m), continuing at £167.452m in 2027/28 and £99.697m in 2028/29. Major projects include the Our City Our River project, schools new builds and extensions, highways and transport improvements, the Guildhall project, and delivery of 311 new affordable homes through the HRA over the forecast period. These large schemes drive the CFR growth and borrowing requirements.
findings.matters: Large capital programmes require substantial financing through borrowing, grants and reserves, directly impacting CFR growth, future revenue costs and borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital programme: Total £226.272m (GF £177.419m, HRA £48.853m); Major schemes: Our City Our River £78.383m, Schools £73.001m, Highways and Transport £41.395m, Guildhall £25.830m
findings.quote: Major schemes: Our City Our River £78.383m, Schools – New Builds/extensions £73.001m, Highways and Transport £41.395m, Guildhall Project £25.830m

findings.headline: Financing costs forecast to rise to 9% of net revenue stream by 2028/29, from 7% in 2025/26
findings.detail: The proportion of the Council's net revenue stream consumed by financing costs (interest and minimum revenue provision) is forecast to increase from 7% in 2025/26 to 8% in 2026/27 and reach 9% by 2028/29. In absolute terms, annual financing costs are forecast to rise from £23.367m to £38.729m over this period. This rising cost burden reflects the impact of higher interest rates and the capital programme's funding requirements on the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Financing costs at 9% of net revenue represent a material and growing call on the revenue budget, reducing flexibility for service spending and increasing the authority's financial vulnerability to interest rate volatility.
findings.figures: Financing costs: £23.367m (2025/26), forecast £32.620m (2026/27), £35.900m (2027/28), £38.729m (2028/29); as percentage of net revenue stream: 7%, 8%, 8%, 9%
findings.quote: Proportion of net revenue stream 7% 8% 8% 9%

findings.headline: Forecast shows cumulative need for £439.9m new external borrowing by 2031/32 as internal resources deplete
findings.detail: The liability benchmark, which estimates the Council's minimum external borrowing requirement, forecasts that new borrowing will be needed progressively: £104.4m by March 2028, rising to £224.1m by March 2029, and cumulating to £439.9m by March 2032. This reflects the Council's transition from using internal reserves to fund capital investment towards reliance on external borrowing as reserves decline from £313.2m to £157.6m over the six-year period.
findings.matters: Large future borrowing requirements have material implications for interest cost, refinancing risk, and revenue budget sustainability; lenders need visibility of forward borrowing plans and the Council's dependence on market access.
